reason: The sources provide over 10 cross-referenced claims from Wikipedia and NASA technical documents detailing the light flashes, cosmic ray causes, and ALFMED experiment.
story: During the Apollo lunar missions, astronauts closing their eyes to sleep in deep space witnessed something uncanny: brilliant flashes of light, streaks, and exploding stars slicing across their darkness. Even with their eyelids shut tight, the flashes kept coming every few minutes. NASA realized invisible, high-energy cosmic rays were zipping straight through the spacecraft hull and penetrating the astronauts' heads, striking their eyes directly. To solve the mystery, astronauts on Apollo 16 and 17 strapped on ALFMED—a bulky helmet lined with radiation-sensitive emulsion plates. By matching cosmic ray track lines on the plates with the exact seconds astronauts reported seeing flashes, scientists proved that cosmic particles were directly ionizing the retina and triggering visual phosphenes.
angle: Apollo astronauts saw phantom light flashes right through their closed eyelids in deep space, caused by cosmic rays blasting directly through their eyeballs.

claims.claim: Apollo astronauts reported visually perceiving spontaneous flashes of light during deep space lunar missions.
The visual light flashes were observed when astronauts were in the dark or had their eyes closed.
High-energy cosmic rays traversing the astronaut's eye or head cause the visual phenomena.
Cherenkov radiation emitted as cosmic ray particles pass through the eye's vitreous humor was proposed as a mechanism for the flashes.
Direct ionization or stimulation of retinal receptors by radiation was identified as a primary cause of the visual flashes.
NASA scheduled dedicated light flash observation sessions during Apollo flights.
NASA deployed a specialized headgear apparatus called ALFMED to investigate the cosmic ray light flashes.
The ALFMED experiment was conducted on board the Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 missions.
The ALFMED device was designed to be worn on the astronaut's head like a helmet with a face shield.
ALFMED contained cosmic-radiation-sensitive emulsion plates to record tracks of particles passing through the astronaut's head.
Particle tracks recorded in the ALFMED emulsions were correlated with the exact times astronauts reported seeing flashes.
Apollo astronauts observed light flashes at a higher frequency during the transit to the Moon than on the return trip to Earth.

disputed: Whether Cherenkov radiation is the dominant cause: S2 notes Cherenkov light is likely too faint to explain most flashes, whereas S1 notes Cherenkov radiation is ruled out for some ISS/Mir observations but remains a possible contributor alongside retinal neuron activation (attribute as competing hypotheses).

Whether dark adaptation is required: S2 notes dark adaptation was not necessary, whereas S1 notes flashes were seen most frequently in the dark but occasionally in dim or bright light (attribute as varying light conditions).
